blocks.content: Knowing what a checked exception is takes five minutes. Knowing where to catch it, how to name it, what to put in the message, and how to make sure it never swallows a root cause that takes experience.
This lesson is about the design side: how to structure exception handling across an entire system so failures are informative, recoverable where possible, and never silently lost.
Topics: layered exception design, exception translation, fail-fast vs graceful degradation, global handlers, logging discipline, and the most costly mistakes in production systems.

blocks.content: 1. The three responsibilities of exception handling
blocks.text: 1. The three responsibilities of exception handling

blocks.content: Every exception handling decision in a system boils down to three questions: who detects the failure, who decides what to do about it, and who informs the outside world. Conflating these is the root of most messy exception code.

blocks.content: 1. Layered exception design
A well-designed system organises exceptions in layers that mirror the architecture. Each layer only exposes exception types that make sense at that abstraction level.

The database layer knows about connection failures. The service layer knows about payment failures. The API layer knows about HTTP error codes. None of them leak the details of the layer below to the layer above.
The key rule: each layer catches the exception types from the layer below and re-throws an exception that belongs to its own vocabulary. The controller never catches a SQLException.
The service never catches a raw DatabaseError. The hierarchy stays clean and each layer can be tested independently.
2. Exception hierarchy design
Good exception hierarchies are shallow and domain-driven. One base class per module, a small number of specific subclasses for failure modes that genuinely need different handling.
Callers who want to handle everything catch the base; callers who care about a specific failure catch the subclass.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1781598239426-901882704.png
catch PaymentException for any payment failure catch subclass only when the response differs
Fail-fast vs graceful degradation
Two opposite philosophies for handling failures and both are right in different situations.

["Fail-fast Crash immediately on the first sign of something wrong. Makes bugs visible early, prevents corrupt state from spreading. 
","Right for: invalid constructor arguments, missing required config, programming errors, startup checks.
"]
items: Fail-fast Crash immediately on the first sign of something wrong. Makes bugs visible early, prevents corrupt state from spreading.
Right for: invalid constructor arguments, missing required config, programming errors, startup checks.

blocks.content: Graceful degradation Catch the failure, log it, and continue with a reduced-quality response. Right for: optional external services, non-critical features, user-facing APIs where a partial result is better than nothing.
3. Global exception handlers
No matter how carefully you design per-layer handling, some exceptions escape to the top.
A global handler is the safety net it logs the failure, returns a clean error response to the caller, and prevents a raw stack trace from leaking to end users or API clients.

blocks.content: 2. Logging discipline

Exception handling and logging are inseparable. The most common logging mistake is logging the same exception at multiple layers you get five lines of stack trace in your logs for a single payment failure, all saying slightly different things.
The rule is simple: log once, at the boundary where the exception is finally handled.

["Log at the boundary, once.The layer that handles the exception (not re-throws it) writes the log line. Inner layers translate and re-throw silently.
","Include the original cause.Always pass the root exception as the second argument to the logger log.error(\"msg\", e) so the full stack trace appears in the log.
","Use structured context.Log the relevant IDs alongside the message: account ID, transaction ID, user ID. Makes filtering logs in production 10× faster.
","Never log then re-throw.Writinglog.error(e); throw e;then logging again one layer up produces duplicate stack traces and hides which layer actually owns the problem.
","Never log then swallow.Writinglog.warn(e)and returning a fallback when the failure was actually serious misleads whoever reads the logs into thinking the system handled it gracefully.
","Choose the right log level.ERRORfor failures that need human attention.WARNfor expected degraded states.INFOfor normal but notable events.DEBUGfor trace data. Miscategorised levels drown alert dashboards in noise.
"]

Use structured context.Log the relevant IDs alongside the message: account ID, transaction ID, user ID. Makes filtering logs in production 10× faster.

Choose the right log level.ERRORfor failures that need human attention.WARNfor expected degraded states.INFOfor normal but notable events.DEBUGfor trace data. Miscategorised levels drown alert dashboards in noise.

blocks.content: 3. Exception messages

A good exception message is a first-responder tool. Someone reads it at 2 AM during an incident. It must tell them what happened, which entity was involved, and what value caused the failure without requiring them to read source code.

["Include the offending value:\"Transfer amount -50.0 must be positive\" not just\"Invalid amount\"
","Include the entity ID:\"Account id=4821 not found\" something you can paste into a database query immediately
","State the constraint that was violated:\"Transfer $1500.00 exceeds daily limit $1000.00\" tells you both what happened and why it was wrong
","Never include passwords, tokens, or PII in exception messages they end up in logs, which end up in log aggregators, which are far less secured than your database
","Avoid vague messages:\"Something went wrong\",\"Error occurred\",\"Failed\" these are noise that make log search impossible
"]
items: Include the offending value:"Transfer amount -50.0 must be positive" not just"Invalid amount"
Include the entity ID:"Account id=4821 not found" something you can paste into a database query immediately
State the constraint that was violated:"Transfer $1500.00 exceeds daily limit $1000.00" tells you both what happened and why it was wrong
Never include passwords, tokens, or PII in exception messages they end up in logs, which end up in log aggregators, which are far less secured than your database
Avoid vague messages:"Something went wrong","Error occurred","Failed" these are noise that make log search impossible

blocks.content: 4. Common design mistakes
Mistake 1: exception hierarchy too deep

Five levels of inheritance for exceptions that all end in the same log line. If you never catch the subclass differently from the parent, the subclass adds nothing. Keep hierarchies flat  one or two levels below the module base is almost always enough.
Mistake 2: using exceptions for flow control

ThrowingItemNotFoundExceptionto signal "this item simply doesn't exist in a cache lookup" and then catching it one line later to return a default is not exception handling it is a slow, misleading goto. UseOptional, a sentinel value, or a boolean return for expected absence.
Mistake 3: leaking internal exception types across module boundaries

LettingSQLExceptionpropagate from the repository layer to the controller, or letting astd::filesystem::filesystem_errorreach your REST handler, couples layers that should be independent. Always translate at the boundary.
Mistake 4: catching then re-throwing without chaining
In Python,raise PaymentError("failed")inside an except block silently drops the original traceback.

In Java,throw new PaymentException("failed")without passing the caught exception as a cause loses the root. Both make post-incident debugging dramatically harder. Always chain: pass the cause explicitly.
Mistake 5: no global handler in a web service

Any unhandled exception that reaches an HTTP framework without a global handler either returns a raw 500 with a stack trace (security leak) or silently returns a 200 with an empty body (worse). Always wire a catch-all handler that returns a clean error shape and logs the details.
Mistake 6: retry without idempotency check

Catching a timeout and retrying a payment transfer without verifying idempotency can charge a user twice. Transient failures that touch mutable state need a token-based deduplication strategy before the retry is safe.
5. Design checklist

["One base per module Each module or service has its own base exception class. Callers import that, not the implementation details underneath.
","Translate at layer boundaries Catch the lower layer's exception type, throw your own. The root cause travels as a chained cause, not as a leaked type.
","Global safety net Every web service has a catch-all handler that logs the full trace and returns a sanitised error response never a raw stack trace.
","Log once at the boundary Inner layers translate silently. The outermost handler that resolves the exception writes the one log line with context IDs and the original cause.
","Message tells the story Every exception message includes the entity, the offending value, and the constraint violated. No vague strings, no PII.
","Fail-fast on programming errors Null arguments, invalid config, broken invariants throw immediately. Don't let corrupt state propagate silently through the system."]

Translate at layer boundaries Catch the lower layer's exception type, throw your own. The root cause travels as a chained cause, not as a leaked type.
Global safety net Every web service has a catch-all handler that logs the full trace and returns a sanitised error response never a raw stack trace.
Log once at the boundary Inner layers translate silently. The outermost handler that resolves the exception writes the one log line with context IDs and the original cause.
Message tells the story Every exception message includes the entity, the offending value, and the constraint violated. No vague strings, no PII.
Fail-fast on programming errors Null arguments, invalid config, broken invariants throw immediately. Don't let corrupt state propagate silently through the system.
